sources.quote: Por regla general, en keshua las palabras s[on] graves, de modo que llevan el acento en la p[e]núltima sílaba, las monosílabas la llevan en [la] única vocal que tienen; algunas interjeccion[es] lo llevan en la última ej. ¡acacau! ¡que calor[!] sí. El acento es invariable, aunque las palab[ras] que la lleven se unan con afijos para formar palabras compuestas. [right margin of the scan is clipped; bracketed letters restored] ... Debe advertirse, que en los nombres que llevan los [sufi]jos y, niy, el vocativo del singular se diferencia de[l nom]inativo, en que el acento carga sobre la última vo[cal]. Ej. Taitáy padre mio, yahuarníy sangre mía.

sources.note: Confirms the catalog's fixed penultimate rule ('las palabras son graves.. acento en la penúltima sílaba'; monosyllables stressed on their only vowel) and adds exceptions the entry does not state: some interjections are stressed final (¡acacáu!), and the vocative singular of nouns with possessive -y/-niy is stressed on the final vowel (taitáy, yahuarníy). States the accent rule is invariable under suffixation (compounds formed with affixes keep the same rule). No secondary stress, no weight, no tone mentioned. Scan is image-only (Google Books);n

sources.citation: O'Rourke, Erin. 2007. Intonation in Quechua: Questions and analysis. Paper, ICPhS XVI Satellite Workshop 'Intonational Phonology: Understudied or Fieldwork Languages' (organizer Sun-Ah Jun), Saarbrücken. 6 pp. (acoustic study, 10 Cuzco Quechua speakers, Praat F0 analysis).
sources.quote: 'In most Quechua varieties, stress is consistently placed on the penultimate syllable, including in Southern Peruvian Quechua. As suffixes are added to a word, stress remains on the penultimate syllable ('wa.si, wa.'si.pi, wa.si.'ku.na, wa.si.ku.'na.pi) ... In words with more than three syllables, an additional secondary stress may be observed on the initial syllable ... primary stress may shift to the last syllable if one of a series of emphatic suffixes is added.' Results: 'In Cuzco Quechua, primary stress is considered to fall on the penultimate syllable of a word ... a peak (H) is observed
sources.locator: sec. 3 'Stress in Quechua' and sec. 5 'Pitch Accents', Figs. 1-3

sources.quote: 'El acento generalmente cae en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Por lo tanto cuando se añade un sufijo que contiene una vocal, el acento cambia de lugar.' Examples /ˈhamu-j/, /haˈmu-wa-j/, /hamu-ˈwa-j-ʧis/ ... Exceptions: morphemes /puni/, /ˈja/, /ˈʧa/ 'con acentos propios supuestamente irregulares' (e.g. /hamu-wa-j-ʧis-puni-taq-ˈja/), plus /aˈɾi/ 'sí' (Rowe 1950) and /kanˈʧa/. No mention of initial secondary stress.

Nothing on word stress, tone or prominence, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's penultimate rule. tone.quote: Figure 3 shows schematic representations of the two contours observed in the Quechua data. The first contour exhibited high accents on the stressed syllables of each word and a low boundary tone (Figure 3a). [...] We represent this contour as [H* H* L%]. In the second contour there was a flat stretch of low or slightly rising pitch throughout the first element of the IP (the adjective) and a very prominent F0 peak on the stressed syllable of the second word (the noun) (Figure 3b). This contour is repre- sented as [L* LH* L%].
tone.locator: p. 80, sec. 5.2 'Quechua'; summary 'Quechua speakers employed two contour types.. [H* H* L%] and [L* LH* L%]' on p. 81
